items.title: Hostile Inference: Exploiting Docker Model Runner for Container Escapes
items.story_key: story|title:hostile inference exploiting docker model runner for container escapes
items.content_excerpt: Local LLM inference is seeing adoption in default developer workflows, and the tooling that serves those models now ships inside products developers already trust. One of those is Docker Model Runner (DMR), the feature in Docker Desktop that pulls, runs, and serves models locally. In November 2025, we reported ZDI-26-150 / CVE-2026-28400 , a denial-of-service (on macOS) stemming from an unauthenticated argument-injection vulnerability in DMR. A container created with the default set of privileges could overwrite and corrupt the Docker Desktop VM’s data disk. Further analysis, under non-default configurations, turned the same primitive into arbitrary code execution on the host, on both macOS and Windows. In this post, we walk through the full chain: the argument-injection primitive, the host file read/write foothold it grants, how we take partial control of what gets written, and the payoff that turns a constrained file write into arbitrary code execution on the host through Docker Extensions. We then cover two further escapes we found along the way: one from an overly permissive Seatbelt sandbox configuration on macOS, and one that pivots the WSL2 VM-to-host boundary through Docker Extensions. Docker Desktop helps run Docker containers on macOS, Windows, and Linux. Docker Desktop for Windows with Windows containers and Docker Desktop for Linux are out of scope for this blog. Since macOS and Windows don’t come with a Linux kernel to run Linux containers, Docker Desktop ships a LinuxKit VM that hosts the container runtime; on macOS the VM runs using the Apple Virtualization Framework , while on Windows it runs under WSL2 by default. Linux containers and the Docker Engine components (runc, containerd, dockerd) run in the Linux VM. Bridging the gap between the host OS and the VM is a daemon called Docker Backend: com.docker.backend (macOS) or com.docker.backend.exe (Windows). This process is responsible for managing the execution environment and brokering all inter-process communication (IPC) across the VM–OS boundary. DMR lets users pull, run, and serve models over OpenAI-compatible APIs using the same idioms as running containers ( docker model pull , docker model run ). Models are distributed as OCI artifacts through OCI-compliant registries and stored on the host. At the time of our research, DMR would create an instance of llama.cpp’s llama-server for inference tasks. DMR is compiled into the Docker Backend. The detail that makes this interesting: on macO

items.title: AgentRoboCritic: Understanding the Capability of Frontier Agents on Direct Robot Control
items.summary: Frontier multimodal language agents such as GPT-6 Astra have demonstrated strong capabilities in controlling robots directly via low-level numerical actions without high-level primitives. However, existing benchmarks report only episode-level success rates, which show neither how these agents succeed nor where they fail. In this paper, we present a systematic action-level analysis of frontier agents on direct robot control across 12 manipulation benchmarks. We introduce AgentRoboCritic, an intent-grounded critique framework in which the policy agent states a local intent alongside each action, and a critic evaluates the action's outcome and failure mode against this intent. Our action-level analysis demonstrates the promising capabilities of frontier agents on direct robot control, including closed-loop recovery from local execution failures, reliable semantic grounding across diverse scenes, and strong zero-shot manipulation without task-specific adaptation. It also identifies their current limitations, including task-relevant physical execution bottlenecks such as grasping and alignment, and uneven recovery across failure modes. Finally, we validate our critic on a 400-action human-annotated benchmark and release a dataset of 12,844 annotated actions alongside a fine-tuned open-source critic, Muse-Glimmer-30B, whose failure-mode accuracy rises from 32.58% to 74.24%, enabling low-cost action-level analysis.

items.title: GLiDE: A Fast, Calibrated Decision Model Distilled from Reasoning Teachers
items.summary:
Decision models enable fast, confidence-aware decisions by scoring candidate answers in a single forward pass, without generating text or intermediate reasoning. Yet reasoning can substantially improve decision quality, raising the question of whether its benefits can be retained without the cost of generating it. We investigate this question with \textbf{GLiDE}, a family of decision models spanning 0.4B to 27B parameters.
  Building on Qwen hybrid language models, GLiDE enables bidirectional interactions between the context, question, and candidate answers by removing causal masking from full-attention layers. To transfer reasoning capabilities into single-pass inference, we combine soft-target distillation from multiple teachers, including a reasoning model, with progressive post-training on diverse decision tasks. We further explore parameter-free recurrent depth to increase inference-time computation without generating tokens.
  Across five model sizes, GLiDE lies on the performance--parameter Pareto frontier of the Hugging Face \DI{}, with each model outperforming evaluated alternatives of equal or smaller size. \dmtwo{} (27B) achieves a hidden-set score of 71.52, with an expected calibration error of 2.0\% and a median latency of 92.9\,ms on a single GPU. Further checkpoint averaging and parameter-free recurrent depth yield GLiDE~27B, which reaches 73.37 with an expected calibration error of 2.1\%.

items.title: How Much Should an Agent Remember? Deployment Lessons from Self-Distilled Memory for LLM Agents
items.summary: LLM agents on long-horizon tasks fail in recurring, procedural ways. They mis-paginate an API, resolve the wrong entity, or answer when no answer was asked. We built a pipeline that lets an agent learn from its own history. It first mines short \emph{lessons} from the agent's own trajectories, one to three per episode. It then consolidates those lessons into a smaller set of \emph{guidelines}, where each guideline records how many lessons it merged. At inference the agent receives either all guidelines or a selected subset. The pipeline ships in the open-source altk-evolve library and is deployed in IBM's CUGA agent and watsonx Orchestrate platform. We report what we learned building, measuring, and productizing it. Our primary instrument is the AppWorld benchmark, across models spanning 40--92\% baseline task completion. The central finding is that the right amount of memory is a property of the model, not the memory. A strong model keeps improving as guidelines are added. DeepSeek-V3.2 gains +9.5 points of task completion and +16.1 points of scenario completion with its full 191-guideline set. A weak model gains less from the same full set than from a small selected subset. gpt-oss-120b starts at 39.9\% task completion. It reaches 51.2\% with all 199 of its guidelines but 55.4\% (mean of two runs) with a selected subset of about 29. Around that result we report what went wrong: a high-support guideline that backfired, provenance silently dropped during consolidation, a swallowed API error that failed every task while producing a plausible log, and a baseline confound that nearly produced a misleading comparison with a prior method. We distill these into recommendations for teams deploying agent memory.

items.title: Show HN: Bulchimbeon, night watch that keeps your Mac awake while AI agents work
items.story_key: story|title:bulchimbeon night watch that keeps your mac awake while ai agents work
items.content_excerpt: 🪖 불침번 — Your Mac's night-watch soldier. Keeps your Mac awake only while AI agents work. No hooks, no daemon on macOS 13+; a small daemon and tray on Linux. Your Mac's night-watch soldier. A menu bar app that keeps your Mac awake only while your AI coding agents are actually working , then salutes "Shift over!" and lets it sleep. No hooks, no daemon, no installed root helper. One app. macOS 13 and later. On Linux, a small daemon with a command line and a tray icon does the same job: see Linux . Bulchimbeon (불침번) is the night-watch duty in the Korean army: someone stays up all night so everyone else can sleep. A pixel-art private takes that shift for your Mac. 🌐 한국어 · 日本語 · 简体中文 💡 Ideas / 문의 / 建议 🗳️ Which agent do you use it with? Where did you get stuck? Vote and tell us Install: brew install --cask s3onghyun/tap/bulchimbeon — or download the latest macOS zip and move it to /Applications . First launch: from 0.12.6 the app is signed with a Developer ID and notarized by Apple, so it just opens. At most, macOS asks once whether to open an app downloaded from the internet: click Open . When it asks whether Bulchimbeon may send notifications, allow it; notifications then come from Bulchimbeon itself. Their notifications show up as "Script Editor" , because macOS won't grant an unnotarized app notification permission of its own. Updating to 0.12.6 or later removes both. Supported agents: Claude Code · Codex · Gemini CLI · Cursor Agent · Copilot CLI · Aider · OpenCode (and your own custom agents). Paste this into Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI or another coding agent. The agent follows docs/install-for-agents.md and leaves any first-launch prompt from macOS to you. To see the sleep block macOS itself is holding, run pmset -g assertions . While on watch: While idle (no agent working), Bulchimbeon releases its block, so pmset -g assertions | grep -i bulchimbeon prints no Bulchimbeon line. Why not just use caffeinate or Amphetamine? Those are great when you want a manual, fixed wake lock. Bulchimbeon starts and ends the lock around active AI-agent work, so it does not get left on overnight. What does it inspect or send? It uses no hooks. Its only network request is the once-a-day update check , which sends nothing but its version and can be turned off. It observes only your own local process metadata to decide whether a supported agent is working; it never stores or prints process command lines or environment variables. items.title: AlphaXiv opens a public preprint server for AI-authored research papers
items.story_key: story|title:alphaxiv opens a public preprint server for ai authored research papers
items.content_excerpt: alphaXiv connects papers, researchers, and organizations, grounding its answers in the underlying work. A twelve-week archive shows how hundreds of independent AI agents develop research norms, review one another’s work, and expose both collaboration’s promise and its limits. Using an observed outcome, a factual world model can estimate alternative actions in the same hidden disturbance, enabling hindsight planning without paired counterfactual data. World models trained on first-person video and actions can map maze and city layouts in latent space while preserving objects needed for planning. AMI - Advanced Machine Intelligence, Jacob T. Schwartz Professor, CS @ New York University Anyscale, Co-Founder & Executive Chairman @ Databricks, Professor, CS @ UC Berkeley LawZero, Founder and Scientific Advisor @ Mila - Quebec Artificial Intelligence Institute, Canada CIFAR AI Chair @ CIFAR, Full Professor, CS @ Université de Montréal A single text can let frontier models identify its human author, exposing active forum users and blind peer reviewers to de-anonymization without web access or candidate lists. Graph-based nearest neighbor search algorithms like HNSW, DiskANN, NSG, and others have surged in popularity in recent years due to their excellent empirical performance in comparison to space-partitioning methods like IVF data structures and Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH). However, in contrast to LSH and related methods, obtaining strong worst-case theoretical guarantees for graph-based search has proven challenging. In this paper, we prove a strong lower bound that helps explain the lack of progress towards such guarantees. We show that no standard graph-based method (any that runs a variant of greedy search on a flat or hierarchical graph) can achieve sublinear query time for approximate nearest neighbor search in Euclidean space, even for an arbitrarily large approximation factor. On the other hand, we prove that sublinear query time is possible if we allow for Steiner points in the search graph. We obtain bounds comparable to LSH, showing e.g., that graph-based search with Steiner points can solve c c c -approximate nearest neighbor search in Euclidean space with query time O ~ ( n 1 / ( c − 1 ) ) \tilde{O}(n^{1/(c-1)}) O ~ ( n 1/ ( c − 1 ) ) . We complement this result with initial experiments exploring how Steiner points can be incorporated into practical graph-based methods. items.content_excerpt: Claude Docs is a doc editor that you, your teammates, and Claude all work in together. The interesting part is that a Claude session anywhere, from chat to Claude Code, can open the same doc and read, write, and comment in it live, right next to you. We released Docs on September 16, 2026. This post is about the service that runs underneath it. Three weeks before Claude Docs opened to the public, it was running as a proof of concept on a single node, used by a few thousand people inside Anthropic. We were racing toward an ambitious launch date, and our own estimate said we'd see millions of docs within the first few days. We launched on September 16. By September 22, people had created over 4.6 million docs. Across 2 billion requests we saw only 60 server errors, and we never had to roll back. The whole Docs service ran on about 50 memory-optimized pods. But honestly, this only worked because our frontier models have gotten much better recently (I used an internal research model roughly comparable to Claude Fable 5.2). In our experience, they can now stick with one goal through a run like this for weeks, which is what helped us hit launch scale in a tight timeline. A few thousand internal users on one machine told us nothing about whether the service would survive launch, and we obviously didn't have launch traffic to test with. We wanted real evidence to decide how fast we could roll out. So on September 4, about two weeks before launch, I had Claude drive a staging cluster that mirrored production at over a million synthetic docs a day and break core components on purpose. And then... I just left it running (I've included the full cost at the end of this article). My setup was pretty simple. The loop was a session in Claude Code that I left running: pick a scenario, run the harness, read the telemetry, propose a fix, ship it to staging, repeat. That session acted as a coordinator and handed most of the work to sub-agents. In the busiest week, that usually meant about 11 sub-agents running at a time, and 30 at the peak. The coordinator also talked to our internal variant of Claude Tag (beta) via the Slack MCP to learn from other infrastructure teams at Anthropic who had scaled similar services. Their agents checked our scaling approach for pitfalls they’d already hit. Each iteration looked the same. items.title: External sandboxes for coding agents
items.summary:
External sandboxes for coding agents

I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine.

I worked on this project with Prime Radiant, the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects.

My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox.

To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations:

  • external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly.
  • external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance.
  • external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package!

Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code.

The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still running:

I continue to be fascinated by the challenge of safely running untrusted code. This external sandbox pattern provides a neat way to experiment with different approaches.

items.title: Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube)
items.summary:
Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube)

Claire Vo runs ChatPRD, an AI platform that helps product managers "turn an idea into a spec". The product has been live since the GPT-4 era, and Claire has been building it in public for much of that time.

In this YouTube video (see also the accompanying Twitter post) Claire describes the flood of token fraud she has seen from groups abusing the product's free trial, sometimes just to get free AI usage but often to resell tokens or run other commercial enterprises on top of the ChatPRD agent.

I am funding a international Roblox and Fortnite map studio. They run a loop of free trials and promo codes and then tunnel to my agent and use it to build Roblox and Fortnite maps.

Apparently one of the common prompts Claire saw running through her agent involved SVGs of pelicans riding bicycles! Presumably the token scammers are using that to help sniff the underlying models - different model families have a definite signature, and I've used it like this in the past to try and guess the identity of stealth preview models on platforms like OpenRouter.

Claire is winding down her free trials entirely, which sadly looks like the right decision in the face of this abuse.

Neon ranks ahead of comparable models and #3 overall with a score of 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its xhigh thinking level, landing just behind larger, slower models. The model is priced at $3 per million input tokens ($0.15 per million cached input tokens, a 95% discount) and $15 per million output tokens, with a 1 million-token context window. Gemini 4 Neon is rolling out today in the Gemini API in Google AI Studio , Gemini for business (via API and model dropdown), for paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity , and for Pro and Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app . Enterprise work lives in spreadsheets, PDFs, charts, audio, and video. Neon can synthesize across all of these inputs in a single 1 million-token context window and turns inputs into structured deliverables. Independent evaluations rank Neon as one of the top models and on benchmarks like the Vals Index , it ranks #2 (70.9%), and reaches #1 on both the Legal Research Bench and Tax Agent Bench . items.title: ClosureBench: A Benchmark for Reasoning under Closure Assumptions
items.summary: AI agents built on large language models (LLMs) often answer questions from incomplete records. Missing information might be interpreted as unknown or false, depending on the completeness of the source. Current evaluations fail to distinguish these two aspects, as they are usually interwoven with other reasoning demands. We present ClosureBench, a benchmark that tests whether LLMs follow the stated rules for dealing with missing information. Every base scenario is tested under OWA, CWA, and LCWA, and only the treatment of missing information changes between variants. ClosureBench provides a verified base benchmark as well as agent extensions for action choice, source scope, and updates. A model is considered correct on a base scenario only if it provides correct answers in all of its closure variants. Across 960 instances, overall accuracy can mask substantial closure mistakes. Models achieve overall accuracy from 71.18% to 99.86% across replicated runs, but their core switch accuracy, measured on the scenarios whose gold label actually changes with the contract, varies between 18.23% and 99.31%. Large discrepancies emerge under LCWA. For example, some agents choose unknown despite the prompt indicating that missing information should be treated as false. Our findings demonstrate that evaluations of AI agents should not only measure whether agents can reason over existing facts but also whether they use the appropriate assumption when information is absent.

items.title: HabitusMem: Belief Memory over Evolving User Preferences for LLM Agents
items.summary: Personalized LLM agents must act on a user's current preferences, which change across interactions and are rarely stated in full. Existing memory systems store and retrieve content from the interaction history and leave the agent to work out which preferences still hold and where they apply. Such content does not indicate whether a preference is still current or where it applies, so agents often act on outdated or misapplied preferences. We instead treat memory as the assistant's belief about the user. Following Bourdieu's account of habitus as durable but revisable dispositions, we model the user as a latent preference state that every interaction, including the current request, both reveals and updates. The belief summarizes what the history supports about this state, and memory consists of the individual beliefs that bear on the agent's current decision, each with its evidence, scope, and status. We implement this view in HabitusMem, a trained writer that states these beliefs as text records for a frozen agent. Across two agent families, HabitusMem achieves the best results among memory systems on both PersonaMem-v2 and VitaBench 2.0. Controlled analyses show that learned request conditioning drives the answering gain, while auxiliary training tasks improve tool use.

items.summary: LangSmith now offers reporting built for coding agents, along with new capabilities that tie their spend to the pull requests they produce.
items.story_key: story|title:langsmith for coding agents now track spend by outcome
items.content_excerpt: Coding is the largest category of enterprise AI application spend, reaching $34B in 2026 . Every company now wants to know what all that spend returns, but most engineering leaders still can’t give an exact answer to what it's buying. To try to understand coding agent ROI, teams used to look at high-level data like usage analytics and AI consumption, but these don’t provide insight into what tokens actually produce. Answering the ROI question is hard and requires visibility into spend across users and teams, along with a way to connect it to outcomes. We felt this friction firsthand when spend with our own coding agent, Robin, started climbing, and is one of the reasons we built a model router. Now we're excited to offer a practical solution for our customers too. LangSmith now offers reporting built for coding agents, along with new capabilities that tie their spend to the pull requests they produce. This provides a clearer way to calculate the ROI behind coding agent budgets and understand how changes to models and policies impact it. The new LangSmith Agent Platform operates around the agent. Each agent has its own record and belongs to an "agent type" that determines what its dashboard shows, which data it connects to, and how it's evaluated. Coding agents are the first specialized agent type, and present data on pull requests, one of the signs that the agent's work is useful. LangSmith already traces coding agents across model providers, including Claude Code and Codex . With coding agents in LangSmith, the spend in each trace is automatically attributed to pull requests each agent contributed to. The attribution reflects the tasks a coding agent is used for. It covers both cases where a single thread can open several PRs, and where a PR can take several threads to finish, so data in LangSmith reflects what your agents actually accomplished and what it cost. Up until today, LangSmith enabled you to see the cost per trace for any of your coding agents, one trace at a time. This is useful for manual debugging, but doesn't provide visibility into trends across the entire team. The new coding agent overview page aggregates those costs and ties them to the pull requests your agents worked on. The dashboard shows KPIs at a glance, and clicking any metric opens its trend over time. For example, if your team switched models, you can compare before and after to see the impact of the change. items.title: Why agent governance starts with observability
items.summary: A strong AI agent governance strategy
items.story_key: story|title:why agent governance starts with observability
items.content_excerpt: AI applications can range from simple internal chatbots to customer-facing, mission-critical agents, but all LLM-based solutions have the capacity to reason independently, so establishing governance has become a key consideration for any degree of AI adoption. Recent headlines on agent security breaches have driven even greater urgency to set up governance as a prerequisite for AI usage and development. While the need for agent governance is widely recognized in most organizations, most are still figuring out where to start. There is some top-down guidance on agent governance from governing bodies, such as the OWASP Agentic AI Threats & Mitigations , NIST AI Risk Management Framework , or AI Agents under EU Law . These guidelines outline agent risks, but don’t define how to mitigate these issues or verify that governance is working. When teams we work with are shipping agents with governing standards in place, we see two main strategies in common among them: Centralizing visibility across agents. Organizations need a central view of the agents running across the company, so costly operations, unauthorized usage, and rogue agents don't fall through the cracks. This visibility makes it possible to establish limits on agents and audit their behavior to verify that guardrails are upheld. Understanding individual agent behavior. Agents are non-deterministic, so the same agent can take different paths and call different tools on the same input. The issues that surface are often specific to each agent's task and execution path, so teams need access to the full trajectory of each agent run to understand its actions and alert on unexpected behavior. At the core of both of these strategies is agent observability , the ability to record, inspect, and analyze every step of your AI agent takes. This typically means tracing the steps and attributes of your agent, having the ability to query and access this data readily, and leveraging capabilities to interpret the agent behavior at scale. Observability is the cornerstone for governance strategies because a guardrail or spend/usage limit doesn't guarantee an agent will follow it, and agents need to be accurately monitored to verify that those guardrails work as intended. The metrics from observability then provide the data to continuously harden overall governance posture. We can think of agent governance methods at a company as either preventative or detective. Preventative governance: Guardrails enforced at runtime to

items.content_excerpt: Explore a new Project Genie experience for Google AI Ultra subscribers, featuring Genie 4, the Project Genie agent, and a community gallery. We are rolling out Genie 4 to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, offering more responsive, social, and interactive world generation. You can now use natural language to edit environments in real time, add native audio, and share your creations in our new community gallery. Visit the Project Genie website to start building your own worlds or join the waitlist if you are a Google AI Pro member. Earlier this year we introduced Project Genie , an experimental research prototype that lets you generate and explore interactive worlds. Early testers told us they wanted deeper control over what happens inside those worlds, and easier ways to build and share them. So today, we are rolling out a new Project Genie experience to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, making these worlds far more responsive, creative, and social. This update unlocks first-time access to Genie 4, new upgrades to Genie 3, the Project Genie agent which helps users build their vision, and a community gallery to discover, explore, and remix worlds. Project Genie brings together our most advanced world models alongside our Gemini models, empowering you to generate, step inside, and shape worlds directly from your browser. With Genie 4 , our most realistic and interactive world model yet, you can now prompt mid-session to change the world you created. Just type a new prompt while you navigate your world and you can edit your environments in real time. Shift the weather, drop in a character, or redirect the action. For the first time, Genie 4 pairs these visuals with real-time native audio that adapts as the scene unfolds, from ambient soundscapes to character dialogue. While Genie 4 delivers our highest-fidelity visuals, physics, and native audio, Genie 3 remains available in Project Genie’s model picker when you want longer runs or panorama-seeded spaces. items.title: claude-code v2.1.328
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added auto mode for Claude Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry and Claude apps gateway; interactive sessions with no permission mode start in it
  • Added "onFailure": "block" for mcp_tool hooks, as for command and HTTP hooks: a hook whose call fails blocks the action
  • Added a warning when a message from a session that skips permission prompts may be held and dropped by a cloud session
  • Added a notice in /status and claude doctor when an OpenTelemetry exporter has no endpoint and its data would likely be lost
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_DEFERRED_TOOL_RESUME, which lets a host stop claude -p --resume and --continue from running a tool call that a hook deferred
  • Added support for apps that embed Claude Code to switch on the policy plugin's allowManagedModsOnly option; an admin's managed settings still win
  • Added a startup warning to the Claude apps gateway when a policy's maxEffortLevel is not a valid effort level
  • Self-hosted runner: Added --repository-folder to name the folder that sessions use for a repository at --capacity 1, in place of its path under the base folder, which can't be a symbolic link
  • Self-hosted runner: Added a start-up warning when the host's settings.json sets a default permission mode that sessions ignore
  • Self-hosted runner: Added --hook-label to claude self-hosted-runner orchestrator, to hand chosen session labels to the spawn-runner hook
  • Self-hosted runner: Added --metadata key=value to claude --environment, to label a session for the spawn-runner hook
  • Self-hosted runner: Added claude_code_self_hosted_orchestrator_session_queue_wait_by_reason_seconds to the orchestrator's /metrics, so a re-opened session's wait can be told from a new one's
  • Self-hosted runner: Added an orchestrator metric, claude_code_self_hosted_orchestrator_sessions_given_up_total, that counts by cause how often Anthropic gave up starting a runner for a session
  • Fixed Bash commands in zsh stopping with a "not found" error at a word that starts with =, such as echo ==== or [ a == b ]; =cmd no longer expands to a command's path
  • Fixed automatic compaction reusing the session's earlier system prompt instead of rebuilding it the way /compact does
  • Fixed markdown rendering freezing on some very long or malformed input
  • Fixed rare screen freezes
  • Fixed Esc often being lost at a permission prompt or question when you typed straight after it; in terminals that send Alt as Esc and a key, an unused Alt or Option key now declines there
  • Fixed a paste or a terminal's reply being typed into the prompt when a slow connection cut it in two
  • Fixed saving a scheduled task erasing the project's other saved tasks when the scheduled tasks file can't be read, on third-party providers or with telemetry or feature flags turned off
  • Fixed a scheduled task with a typo in the project's scheduled tasks file being deleted the next time that file was saved
  • Fixed a case where a resumed cloud session could lose its compaction summary or recent messages when a message was saved late
  • Fixed the token counts on the spinner and for subagents counting a retried reply twice, missing replies that were not streamed, and standing still while Claude thinks
  • Fixed the error shown when usage credits run out mid-response, which named a rate limit
  • Fixed auto mode failing every turn outside Claude Desktop with CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_EXPERIMENTAL_BETAS set behind a gateway rejecting betas, on Bedrock, Agent Platform, Foundry or Claude apps gateway
  • Fixed CLAUDE_STREAM_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS not lengthening the 5-minute connection limit on gateways, custom base URLs and cloud providers
  • Fixed some Claude Desktop sessions on third-party providers, other than scheduled tasks, ending for good with "Prompt is too long" after large tool results; the largest are now left out
  • Fixed MCP tools whose input schema starts with anyOf, oneOf or allOf going missing on third-party providers or with telemetry or feature flags turned off
  • Fixed an MCP tool with an invalid input schema failing requests on third-party providers or with telemetry or feature flags turned off; the tool is now left out and Claude is told why
  • Fixed effort being turned off for a subagent's model for the session if Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform or Foundry refused its progress summary's effort setting (regression in 2.1.327)
  • Fixed Code Mode stopping a script when a permission prompt outside auto or bypass mode, a plan approval or a question stayed open for ten minutes
  • Fixed Code Mode scripts in auto and bypass-permissions modes failing to call an MCP server that had connected while the previous script was running
  • Fixed Code Mode scripts not running in the background in auto or bypass permissions mode in a session chosen in the claude --resume picker
  • Fixed Code Mode losing a loaded skill, hook context or a note typed with a permission approval when resuming a session in which one reply ran several scripts
  • Fixed Claude not being told that a Code Mode script was cut off when the session was resumed from the picker or in a mode that asks for permission
  • Fixed Code Mode silently using undefined for top-level variables that an earlier failed script never set
  • Fixed Code Mode scripts not being told when a failing command's long output was cut
  • Fixed Code Mode refusing valid scripts that start with a { block
  • Fixed Code Mode refusing scripts that use both a top-level await and a top-level return
  • Fixed an @-mentioned small file not being attached in Code Mode after a script had read or written it
  • Fixed Code Mode offering write() and edit() to read-only subagents that can't call them
  • Fixed Claude starting a turn by itself in Code Mode when Esc was followed by a command such as /model
  • Fixed Claude in Code Mode not being told to run workflows only when you ask, or the workflow size you set in /config
  • Fixed Remote Control repeating the same disconnect message, and telling you to retry a session that can't reconnect
  • Fixed a waiting permission prompt being lost, and its answer ignored, when a remote session restarted while the service was slow
  • Fixed cloud sessions resuming a cleared conversation after a rewind followed by /clear
  • Fixed a remote session losing a turn's tool calls and results when its runner or worker was lost after a dropped model stream had been retried
  • Fixed cloud and Remote Control sessions that just started, or have an @ in their title, being unreachable in cross-session messaging from a session with Remote Control on
  • Fixed Claude being told that cloud sessions can never reply; it now learns when a reply can come and how else to get the result
  • Fixed /diff, the Changes pane of Remote Control sessions and the diff beside an edit leaving out committed work after a command moved into another repository
  • Fixed Remote Control not showing a running workflow's agents when a session run by an IDE extension or other SDK app is opened over an hour after the workflow last made progress
  • Remote Control: Fixed an idle Desktop or VS Code session showing as running after Remote Control is turned on
  • Fixed the model saying background agents were still running after an SDK interrupt had stopped them
  • Fixed Send now in the desktop app and SDK hosts telling Claude that a stopped web search found no results
  • Fixed Cmd+letter being typed into the prompt in terminals that report Cmd
  • Fixed Ctrl+click opening a link twice in GNOME Terminal, side mouse buttons acting as clicks, and the first wheel notch in the other direction being ignored after a pause, in fullscreen mode
  • Fixed Shift+Enter in Konsole outside tmux and ssh, and Alt shortcuts on non-Latin keyboard layouts in terminals that speak the kitty keyboard protocol
  • Linux: Fixed pasting in other apps freezing while Claude Code is suspended with Ctrl+Z, when xclip or wl-copy is installed
  • Linux: Fixed Ctrl+V missing the clipboard image, pasting an old one or hanging
  • Fixed text copied in fullscreen mode including the quote bar, losing spaces at line wraps when a drag scrolled upward, or missing words under the "Jump to bottom" pill
  • Fixed an image path pasted into a ! command becoming an attachment
  • Fixed Ctrl+C showing no exit warning while the ? shortcuts list is open
  • Fixed Ctrl+R search in fullscreen mode and the /theme color editor picking the wrong row when keys arrive together, and keys being dropped there and in the search of /config and /plugin
  • Fixed wrong or missing colors inside GNU screen
  • Fixed many background notifications cutting into the top border of open dialogs in fullscreen mode
  • Fixed a message to a background agent showing a long file path in place of a pasted image
  • Fixed /goal removing a skill's Stop hook, or ending early on another hook's result, when both had the same wording
  • Fixed /bug saying cancelled after the report was sent
  • Fixed Esc not dismissing the transcript share question for Pro and Max users
  • Fixed /hooks losing your place when going back
  • Fixed /export writing a file named .txt when the name was left empty
  • Fixed /terminal-setup in Zed replacing a symlinked keymap.json with a plain file
  • Fixed /install-github-app adding a code review workflow when asked to update the existing workflow file
  • Fixed /plugin reopening a skill, or closing the open page, when a slow save or removal finished after you went back
  • Fixed /plugin asking to uninstall the wrong plugin, or ignoring Esc, after leaving a plugin while a change was still running
  • Fixed typing and arrow keys not working on the /plugin Installed tab after a search with no results or a click on the tab row
  • Fixed holding Enter in /plugin turning off several installed plugins
  • Fixed the /usage plugin total stopping at 2,000 tokens on 1M context models, and low token estimates in /usage and /plugin when no model is picked
  • Fixed Esc on the Bedrock access keys step closing /login instead of going back
  • Fixed /exit and Ctrl+D describing running work differently, and /exit warning about a workflow that had stopped
  • Fixed Claude calling an artifact private after reading one in a shared folder or publishing to another organization's, and saying only named people can open one when its folder's people can too
  • Fixed a plugin's toast sometimes showing another plugin's text
  • Fixed a mod saved just after a turn began sometimes reloading mid-turn instead of at the turn's end
  • Fixed one malformed OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES entry dropping the variable's other labels from metric points, events, and spans. Now only that entry is left off
  • Fixed agent hooks running past their timeout while compacting after a request was refused as too large
  • Fixed a crash at startup when FORCE_COLOR is set to a negative number
  • Fixed a crash in secret masking when the machine is almost out of memory
  • Fixed the Bash sandbox on Linux renaming .git/HEAD after each command when the branch name is not valid UTF-8
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed all running sessions being stopped when a proxy or web filter answered a poll with HTTP 200 and a body such as {}; the runner now retries such a poll
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed deletion of a kept clone's objects or refs, and of commits that existed only there, after a temporary disk error; that start now fails instead
  • Fixed self-hosted runners stopping when their token ran out on a host whose clock is slow or was set back
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed sessions with Anthropic-managed git losing git access to GitHub after a script or hook in the session ran claude again
  • Fixed self-hosted runners with Anthropic-managed git being unable to fetch or push where the machine's git config sets http.proactiveAuth
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a runner that exited without telling the server when setup failed after it had registered; it now deregisters with a reason, and an on-demand runner reports the failed start
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed archiving or requeueing a session not taking effect while it waited for another session to prepare the same repository (--capacity above 1)
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a session with a damaged .claude.json failing every later start under --trust-workspace false; it now starts on defaults, with MCP servers turned off there on again
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a failed start's message losing the words that say what failed when a checkout hook or git printed a lot
  • Fixed the self-hosted runner skipping its post-session hook when a disk stalled for a few seconds; on a dead disk a session's end can take 25 seconds longer by default
  • Fixed self-hosted runners: a session that resumes in a new Claude config directory no longer loses its task list
  • Fixed Claude not being told when a self-hosted session starts without one of its repositories, and why
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed --correlation-id of claude --environment not reaching the spawn-runner hook
  • Fixed the self-hosted runner setup wizard's key rotation advice, which now warns that revoking a key stops the sessions running under it
  • Improved claude -p and SDK sessions to fetch managed-settings plugins that have their own git repository, in the background, for a later session
  • Improved how soon managed-settings plugins from a git marketplace load on a fresh machine in claude -p, SDK and Claude Desktop sessions; a short run may exit up to 30 seconds later
  • Improved the time to resume large sessions
  • Improved memory use when resuming a session with many images
  • Improved memory use and response time in long SDK and desktop sessions that run slow commands or tools
  • Improved Code Mode's speed in auto and bypass-permissions modes by removing a 0.75 second pause after most scripts
  • Improved prompt caching for new Code Mode sessions that have MCP servers, and Claude is now told when a server is still connecting and when the list of servers changes
  • Improved Code Mode's token use with shorter tool descriptions
  • Improved Code Mode to show the command a script is running, and its output, while it runs
  • Improved Code Mode edits: an edit that changes nothing no longer stops a script, and Claude is told where a failed edit matches or comes closest
  • Improved Code Mode: Claude is now told which tool calls were still running when a script failed
  • Improved how Claude starts dev servers in Code Mode's auto and bypass modes: Claude is told to run them as background tasks that show in /tasks
  • Windows: Improved Code Mode by telling Claude that scripts' shell commands run in Git Bash and that PowerShell aliases run instead of functions with the same name
  • Improved starting several in-process teammates at once: far fewer now fail with "Lock file is already being held"
  • Improved the computer use approval dialog: it now shows each app's level of access and plainer warnings
  • Improved cross-session messaging: Claude now explains that Remote Control is off when a cloud session or another computer is not listed
  • Improved claude -p text output to say on stderr when a message from another session is held or dropped, and how to allow it
  • Improved Claude's answers on who can open an artifact it published: Claude is now told to check the artifact again instead of repeating the last publish's answer
  • Improved resumed self-hosted runner sessions: Claude now checks whether its earlier work is still there, and says what is missing
  • Changed plan mode and Bash prompts for Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 on third-party providers to use and offer auto mode, as on newer models; disableAutoMode turns both off
  • Changed Code Mode to no longer run UserPromptSubmit hooks, managed ones included, on scripts' output; to redact that output, use a PostToolUse hook with updatedToolOutput
  • Changed /code-review on most models to report only bugs and CLAUDE.md violations; run /simplify for reuse, simplification and efficiency cleanups
  • Changed /code-review to mark each finding Important, Pre-existing or Nit on most models, and to end each summary with a suggested fix; a clean review's list now reads "Code review found no issues."
  • Changed deniedMcpServers entries of the form claude.ai <name> to apply to that connector in cloud and self-hosted runner sessions too
  • Changed managed PostToolUse hooks to no longer fire for calls refused before they ran: no log entry, rewrite, block or stop there; PostToolBatch gets most, not marked as refused
  • Changed /bug to ask Yes or No before sending, so repeated Enters no longer send a report or open GitHub
  • Changed subagents in claude -p, the Agent SDK, desktop and VS Code to wait for their own subagents by default when CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT=0 is set
  • Changed claude -p with CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT=0 to count a background subagent and those it waits for against one 10-minute wait; raise CLAUDE_CODE_PRINT_BG_WAIT_CEILING_MS for longer chains
  • Changed a shell command rewritten by a PermissionRequest hook to a sandbox-excluded command to run outside the sandbox
  • Changed the Claude in Chrome welcome screen and /chrome to say that Claude Code asks before Claude acts on a site, unless your permission mode or a rule in /permissions answers
  • Changed Claude Desktop and Agent SDK sessions on third-party providers or with telemetry or feature flags off to end the turn when closed with a question open, instead of continuing without an answer
  • Changed pasted text to be marked for Claude as pasted, on third-party providers or with telemetry or feature flags turned off
  • Changed subagent progress summaries in terminal sessions on the Anthropic API to be written by the default small fast model from short notes, also with telemetry off, using far fewer tokens
  • Changed how a sandbox that can't start is reported, unless sandbox.failIfUnavailable is set: the next sandboxed Bash command is refused and says that the sandbox is off for the session
  • Changed /list-agents to show its list to you alone; Claude lists sessions itself when needed
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed the built-in gh api to be off by default where settings guard Claude's GitHub tools by name; --use-anthropic-gh true turns it on
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed a claude that a wrapper script runs before the session's own claude is up, or after it has ended, to have no Anthropic-managed git
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed CLAUDE_RUNNER_SESSION_UUID and CLAUDE_CODE_REMOTE_SESSION_UUID to both be set for the session and its checkout, post-session and spawn-runner hooks
  • Changed self-hosted runners at --capacity 1 to refuse a session earlier when the path of a repository it pushes to is a symbolic link
  • [VSCode] Added a notice when a message from another session is held, with a link to the settings file that can allow it
  • [VSCode] Fixed the permission prompt cutting off its No button, reply field or title when the panel is low or a command, URL or description is long
  • [VSCode] Fixed failed or blocked tool calls showing no reason or a reason cut short, and Glob and Grep counting an error as results

items.title: An updated Clairic and Clairic-flash are now open-weight, from the new Workers AI Superintelligence team
items.summary: Clairic graduates from preview, while Clairic-flash joins the repertoire on Workers AI. We’re doing an open-weight release for both extraction models.
items.story_key: story|variant:flash|title:an updated clairic and clairic flash are now open weight from the new workers ai
items.content_excerpt: Cloudflare has become a neolab. We’re building our own frontier AI models for our customers and the open-source community. Both extraction models are hosted on Workers AI and full open weights are available on Hugging Face . We’re also excited to re-introduce ourselves as the Workers AI superintelligence team, the frontier AI research team behind Clef , Clairic, and lots more in the works. This team is working quickly to push the AI frontier and build useful models for Cloudflare’s customers and the open source community. Since announcing Clairic in preview, we have received a ton of use cases and helpful feedback on how customers wanted to use an extraction model. We heard about use cases ranging from extracting data from images like receipts to reading values from support tickets. We knew that we wanted extraction to be the clear focus for the model, so it had to excel at reading from unstructured data. We decided to go back to the drawing board with Clairic and redesigned our architecture, differentiating this new version of Clairic from our preview release. For ordinary text and number extraction fields, we now use parallel slot autoregressive generation instead of a single forward pass. Each field uses the tokens it has already written to choose its next token, then stops at its own end marker. All the fields advance together in the serving batch, still giving lightning-fast latency per request. This boosted our accuracy in extraction for both text and images, and the trade-off in accuracy offsets the small latency cost. For computation, estimation, and extraction use cases, we trained special heads that can handle estimates, forecasts, durations, calculated dates, and explicit arithmetic. Although the model architecture evolved, we kept the parts of the typed API interface that make the answers useful: confidence scores, character spans, and probabilities are still intact with every request. The model is still incredibly fast and cheap. From the evals below, you can see how our newer versions of Clairic have greatly improved on extraction across text, images, PDFs, and more. There are no public extraction benchmarks yet, but we ran our internal evals for other emerging extraction models on the market, such as Liquid AI’s D1.2 (pipelined with Apple Vision for optical character recognition) and Scaledown’s Extract . Our Clairic models excel across extraction use cases, but take these evals as directional guidance since they are self-reported. We wanted
